turns.content: ok so, julian secretly added my dad to the guest list a month ago. i was no contact, he knew. i found out last week, canceled the catering, got my three grand back. now they're all saying i ruined the wedding. 80 people no dinner. but julian did this. i just protected myself. was that not the right call.

Okay, two things are true at once here, and the people yelling at you are only looking at one of them.

**Julian did the actually serious thing.** You were no contact. He knew. He put your dad on the list anyway and kept it from you for a month. That's not a mix-up or an overstep, that's him deciding he knows better than you about your own safety and then hiding it so you couldn't object. If anyone "ruined" something, it's the person who blew up your trust a few weeks before you're supposed to marry him. Your anger is completely earned.

**But the catering cancellation doesn't really protect you.** Your dad's still on the list. Julian still did what he did. What got removed is dinner for 80 people who had nothing to do with any of this. So when you say "I just protected myself," I'd gently push on that. It reads more like you needed to grab back control of *something*, fast, after finding out you'd been steamrolled. That's an incredibly human response, and I get it. It's just not the same as protection, and I think you know that, or you wouldn't be asking.

The hard part is that the catering fight is a decoy. The real question is sitting underneath it: do you still want to marry someone who'll override a boundary that big and lie about it? Whatever the answer, that's where the energy needs to go, not into whether the chicken gets served.

A couple things I'd want to know if I were sitting across from you: Has Julian actually taken your dad off the list, or is he still defending it? And is the wedding still on as far as you're concerned, or is that up in the air too? Those answers change what "the right call" even looks like from here.
ok so, are you saying i'm basically as bad as ray. because that's what it sounds like.

No. I'm not saying that, and I want to be really clear about it because I get why it landed that way.

Ray hurt you badly enough that you cut him out of your life. That's a person who did damage over years and left you having to protect yourself from him. What you did last week was cancel a dinner. Those aren't in the same universe. Nobody's going no-contact with you over chicken.

What I said was that the catering move didn't actually protect you, it just gave you something to control in a moment when Julian had taken control away from you. That's a critique of one decision made under pressure. It is not a verdict on who you are. People who've been hurt the way you have often reach for the nearest lever when they feel cornered, and that's a stress response, not a character flaw.

And I'll say it again so it doesn't get lost: the person who created this situation is Julian. He knew, he did it anyway, he hid it. Everything after that, including the cancellation, is fallout from his choice. The fact that other people are pointing at you instead of him says more about how uncomfortable they are with the real problem than about you.

I think the "am I as bad as Ray" question is telling, though. If that's where your head went, it sounds like you're carrying a fear that any time you react strongly, you're turning into him. Is that something Julian or your family has said to you before?
ok so, the 80 guests. julian invited them, julian can feed them. why is that on me.

Because you're the one who canceled it. That's the plain answer, and it's why people are pointing at you. Not because you're the villain, but because the last hand on the lever was yours.

Here's where I think you're partly right, though. Those 80 people aren't Julian's guests. They're *your* guests, plural. It's your wedding too. So "Julian invited them, Julian can feed them" doesn't quite hold, because you didn't get pulled into someone else's party. You're co-host. If the wedding happens, feeding the room is a shared problem no matter whose credit card the deposit came from.

But flip it around: if Julian wants this wedding to go forward after what he pulled, then yeah, he can step up and figure out food. That's not you dumping it on him unfairly, that's the natural cost of blowing up your partner's trust a few weeks out. He created the crisis, he can do some of the sweating. You're allowed to say "I'm not spending another three grand on a day you sabotaged, so you solve dinner." That's a reasonable position.

What doesn't work is "it's not on me at all." You're in this thing. You either want the wedding, in which case you're on the hook for making it function alongside him, or you don't, in which case the guest problem evaporates because there's no wedding.

So I'd stop arguing about who owes the chicken and ask yourself the thing you keep stepping around: is this wedding still happening? Everything else sorts itself out once you know that.

ok so, alternatives. i could attend and just avoid ray. or give julian 48 hours to uninvite him. or arrange a cheap group dinner myself. all of those felt like caving. was instant cancellation the only self-respecting move.

No. And I think you've got "self-respect" and "biggest possible reaction" tangled together, which is really common when you grew up around someone like Ray.

Look at your list again:

**Attend and avoid Ray.** Yeah, this one is caving. You'd be swallowing your boundary to keep the peace on the biggest day of your life, and Julian would learn that overriding you works. Your gut was right to reject it.

**Give Julian 48 hours to uninvite him.** This is the one. It's the most self-respecting option on the board. You'd be saying: "This is non-negotiable, here's the line, here's the deadline, and the consequences are on you if you don't fix it." That's not caving. That's a person who knows exactly what they will and won't accept and gives the other person one clean chance to choose. If he'd refused, *then* you cancel everything, and nobody could say a word. If he'd folded, you'd have your boundary intact, dinner intact, and a very clear read on whether he can course-correct when he's wrong.

**Arrange a cheap dinner yourself.** This is you absorbing the cost of his mess. Not caving exactly, more like cleaning up after him. Not great, but not shameful either.

The reason the ultimatum felt like caving is that it involves waiting, and waiting felt like weakness. But there's a difference between reacting instantly and holding firm. Ray, from what you've described, sounds like someone who reacts instantly. The people who have real self-respect can say "here's my line" and then hold still, because they're not afraid of the answer.

The cancellation was understandable. I'm not going to pretend it was the only strong move, though. The strongest move was the one that put the decision back in Julian's hands and made him show you who he is.

And here's the thing: that door isn't closed. You can still say, "Ray gets uninvited by Friday, or I'm done." The chicken's already gone. The real question never was.
ok so, heading in now. what do i actually own tonight. julian's manipulation, yes. the guests going hungry, do i own any of that or not.

Yes, you own a piece of it. Not the whole thing, and not the part people are trying to hand you, but a piece.

Here's the split as cleanly as I can put it:

**Julian owns:**
- Putting Ray on the list knowing you were no contact.
- Hiding it for a month.
- Creating the crisis that everything else fell out of.
- Fixing the Ray problem. That's his, full stop.

**You own:**
- Choosing the nuclear option when a firmer, slower one was available. You had the 48-hour move and you skipped it.
- The fact that 80 people currently have no dinner because of a decision you made, not one he made.
- Being part of the solution if the wedding goes forward. Not paying for it necessarily, but you don't get to fold your arms and say "not my problem."

**You don't own:**
- Being "the person who ruined the wedding." That framing is people avoiding the harder conversation about Julian.
- Any guilt about protecting yourself from Ray. That was always legitimate.
- Feeling like a bad person for reacting hard when you'd just been blindsided.

If it helps, here's a version you can actually say tonight: *"I canceled the catering because I felt cornered and needed to do something. That was the wrong lever and I'll help fix dinner. But I'm not the one who created this. You put Ray on the list and hid it. That's the thing we actually need to talk about, and he's off the list or I'm out."*

Owning your part first makes it way harder for anyone to dodge his. You're walking in there with clean hands, not because you did nothing wrong, but because you're the only one willing to say what you did.

You've got this. Go slow, say the thing, don't let the chicken become the headline.
